items.mnemonic_text: A box repeating the same shape inside: the same.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A wide box drops onto the level <radical>ground</radical> right outside Koichi's konbini, three walls up and no floor, blocking the door. You crouch down to peer through its open front — that's exactly the <radical>wide box</radical> you know — and staring back out of the gloom is a <radical>mouth</radical>, yawning out the very order you were about to say yourself, word for word. Same ground, same box, same mouth: same.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at Koichi's konbini, the mouth belongs to the onigiri baker, elbow-deep in <reading>dough</reading> behind the counter. Every time you ask what's going on, he just grunts <reading>どう</reading> without looking up — same shrug, same word, same batch of dough, every single time you ask.

items.mnemonic_text: Legs launching outward from a bow: departure, emitting.

items.reading_mnemonic: On the platform, a conductor named <reading>Hatsu</reading> slams the doors and yells <reading>はつ</reading> into his whistle as steam bursts from the wheels — one word, and the train is already gone.

items.mnemonic_text: One (一) over a white (白) sheet counted a hundred times.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Put the <radical>number one</radical> on top of a ray of light so bright it turns <radical>white</radical>, and look what happens: that single one stacked over the white glow multiplies into a whole crowd. One little stroke sitting above all that whiteness isn't just one anymore — it's a hundred.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a hiccuping cook keeps counting onigiri, and every time he hits a full tray he lets out a huge "<reading>ひゃく</reading>!" — a hiccup and a yell in one, because a hundred rice balls is a lot to hiccup through.

items.mnemonic_text: A slash over ten (十) multiplies it into a thousand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take the plus sign for <radical>ten</radical> and lay a single slash across its top, like one bold pen-stroke scratched over it. That one extra mark turns humble ten into something enormous — you've just multiplied it a hundredfold. Ten with a lid on top means a thousand.
items.reading_mnemonic: A senator named Sen shows up at the shrine and drops a thousand coins into the offering box all at once. "That's from all my constituents," she says, "<reading>せん</reading> of them exactly." Every time you see this kanji, hear Sen bragging about her せん coins.
items.description: Count the horizontals and look at the top. 千 has one bar under a slanting flick. 十 has one bar and no flick, just a straight cross. 午 and 干 both carry two bars — 午 under a flick, 干 starting flat.

items.mnemonic_text: A stylized heart shape with three drips of feeling.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You find the cartoon <radical>heart</radical> on Grandma Kane's mossy steps, left lobe puffed, cleft pinched, point tapping the moss. Shrine cats bat the three leftover beats bouncing in the chambers, and it cannot hold one quiet thought. That jitter is a <radical>heart</radical> and a mind, still mid-thump.
items.reading_mnemonic: You watch Shinny jog up the mossy steps in sandals too big. He misses the bell rope and plants his <reading>shin</reading> on the bronze rim instead, then folds onto the moss groaning <reading>しん</reading> as the leftover beats bounce once for each groan.
items.description: 心 is the cartoon heart: left lobe, cleft, point, and three bouncing beats. 必 is that same heart with one extra diagonal stroke slashing through it.

items.mnemonic_text: A single hooked mark standing for a whole ten thousand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single hook-shaped banner snapping in the wind above a market stall. On that one banner, someone has painted a running tally that just keeps climbing — past a thousand, past nine thousand, until the whole cloth is crammed with zeros. That one impossibly loaded banner stands for ten thousand.
items.reading_mnemonic: A street vendor named Manny throws his arms wide under that banner and yells, "Man, I've sold ten thousand of these!" You can hear the <reading>まん</reading> right there in his ecstatic "Man!" as the crowd surges in.
items.description: 万 and 方 share a horizontal over a hooked stroke. 万 is just those two: a flat bar, then a stroke that drops and hooks left. 方 adds a dot on top and a short slash, so it runs to four strokes against 万's three.

items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the beeping till spits out change, and a friend named En scoops up every round coin, grinning "these <reading>えん</reading> are mine." Every time you hear the till beep, picture En pocketing えん.
items.description: Means yen (Japan's currency) and also circle or round; shows up on money, prices, and words for round shapes.

items.mnemonic_text: Words (言) given a式 (form/ceremony): a formal test.

items.mnemonic_text: Grass on top of a person changing (化): a blooming flower.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A fresh patch of <radical>grass</radical> is sprouting out of the soil the way it always does, two clumps poking up over one line of dirt — except this morning one clump has gone rogue and shot a tall stem straight up with a wide open bloom on the end, petals spilling over sideways. The rest of the grass sits underneath it looking embarrassed. Grass with a blossom bursting out of the top of it is a flower.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, lands right in the middle of the flowerbed and lets out a proud 「<reading>か</reading>」, singeing every petal within reach. Now the only flower left standing is the scorched one under her claws.
items.description: Means "flower"; a very common everyday kanji seen in words for flowers, plants, and blossoms.

example_sentences.japanese: 母に花を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought flowers for my mother.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]に花[はな]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で花を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw flowers at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で花[はな]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: この花は高いです。
example_sentences.english: This flower is expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: この花[はな]は高[たか]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: A person (亻) relying on old (昔) favors: to borrow.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <radical>day</radical>, as the sun climbs behind that little windowpane, a <radical>person</radical> strides in from the left and swipes <radical>two</radical> chopsticks off next door's table — promising to bring them back before the window goes dark again. It isn't stealing if you plan to return it; it's borrowing.
items.reading_mnemonic: The neighbor doesn't even look up. She just hears a stray cat named <reading>Shaku</reading> hiss <reading>しゃく</reading> from the doorway — her signal that her chopsticks have gone wandering again and will be back by dinner.
items.description: 借りる marks the side receiving something on loan — you end up holding an item that isn't yours yet. The opposite motion, handing something over to someone else, is a completely different kanji; don't let the shared idea of a loan blur which direction this one points.

example_sentences.japanese: 兄は銀行からお金を借りました。
example_sentences.english: My older brother borrowed money from the bank.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]は銀[ぎん]行[こう]からお金[かね]を借[か]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館で辞書を借りました。
example_sentences.english: I borrowed a dictionary from the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で辞[じ]書[しょ]を借[か]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 借金は大変です。
example_sentences.english: Debt is tough.
example_sentences.furigana: 借[しゃっ]金[きん]は大[たい]変[へん]です。

items.mnemonic_text: Money (貝) replacing (代) what's missing: to lend.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> strides in from the left, hammers a <radical>stake</radical> into the square, banner flapping, then tips open the clam-shell wallet — coins spilling from the <radical>money</radical> shell into open hands. The flag stays planted as a record of what was handed over, and to whom: this is lending.
items.reading_mnemonic: By the planted stake, a goat named <reading>Tai</reading> headbutts the empty shell and bleats <reading>たい</reading>, annoyed that all the coins are already gone — lent out before she got her share.
items.description: 貸す marks the side handing something over — you're the one giving up temporary use of something. The receiving side of that same transaction is a completely different kanji; keep the direction straight instead of leaning on the shared idea of a loan.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は友達に傘を貸しました。
example_sentences.english: I lent my umbrella to a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]に傘[かさ]を貸[か]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は先生に辞書を貸してもらいました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher lent me a dictionary.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は先[せん]生[せい]に辞[じ]書[しょ]を貸[か]してもらいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行はその会社にお金を貸しました。
example_sentences.english: The bank lent money to that company.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]はその会[かい]社[しゃ]にお金[かね]を貸[か]しました。

items.mnemonic_text: Thread (糸) wound to its winter (冬) finish: to end.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane sits on the shrine steps unspooling a length of <radical>thread</radical>, fibers fraying at the tip, and tied to the very end is a duckling towed along by its <radical>trailing foot</radical>, webbed foot skidding on the mossy stone. The spool runs out, the duckling skids to a stop at her feet, and there is nowhere left to go — that's the end.
items.reading_mnemonic: The instant the thread runs out, one of the shrine cats pounces and clamps its teeth on what's left of the duckling's lace like it's stealing a <reading>shoe</reading> — its triumphant yowl comes out as <reading>しゅう</reading>, the exact sound of the last stretch of thread giving way.

example_sentences.japanese: 宿題はもう終わりました。
example_sentences.english: I already finished my homework.
example_sentences.furigana: 宿[しゅく]題[だい]はもう終[お]わりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 映画の終わりはとても悲しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨はもうすぐ終わります。
example_sentences.english: The rain will be over soon.
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]はもうすぐ終[お]わります。

items.mnemonic_text: A tiny hook with two small dots: small.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single hook standing upright with two dots flanking it, one on each side, like something delicate pinched between two fingertips. It's so slight it could vanish if you sneezed. That tiny hook with its two little dots is the very picture of <radical>small</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, snaps his white glove and shrinks the whole set until the doves look like specks. As everything gets impossibly small, the crowd gasps, "<reading>しょう</reading>!" — the man himself is the smallest thing on stage.
items.description: 小 is three strokes: a hooked vertical with a short dash on each side. 少 is 小 with a fourth stroke, a slash sweeping down to the left beneath it. If there is a tail, it is 少.

example_sentences.japanese: あの小さい猫を見ましたか。
example_sentences.english: Did you see that small cat?
example_sentences.furigana: あの小[ちい]さい猫[ねこ]を見[み]ましたか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の部屋は小さいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、小さい本を買いました。

example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、小[ちい]さい本[ほん]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: Grasping (⺈) at the heart (心): an urgent hurry.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>broom</radical>'s cat sleeps through it, so crumbs and cat skid down the hallway too fast to stop. Someone chasing it yanks the <radical>wrap</radical> tighter around the watermelon, and the jolt sets the <radical>heart</radical> — hook flicking, three drops flung loose — pounding in a full panicked sprint. Everyone hurries.
items.reading_mnemonic: Skidding into that same hallway, a courier pigeon named <reading>Cue</reading> can't stop in time and slams into the pile, wheezing out a strangled <reading>きゅう</reading> as crumbs and feathers go flying. He's always this late, and it's always this loud.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅まで急いでください。
example_sentences.english: Please hurry to the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]まで急[いそ]いでください。

example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]る前[まえ]に、家[いえ]へ急[いそ]ぎましょう。

example_sentences.japanese: 朝、学校へ急いで行きました。

example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]、学[がっ]校[こう]へ急[いそ]いで行[い]きました。

items.mnemonic_text: A hand over a craftsman's tool, held in the left hand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A badger in a hard hat stands on the level <radical>ground</radical> of the <radical>construction</radical> site while the crane lowers the steel I-beam toward its slot. His right hand is busy holding a sandwich, so he steadies the swinging girder with the other one, arm braced flat and taking the whole weight. That steadying hand is the hand on the left.
items.reading_mnemonic: A samurai marches into Koichi's konbini and slams down a coin with his left hand, barking "<reading>さ</reading>!" as he demands the last onigiri. Every time you see this kanji, hear that samurai's sharp さ ringing off the beeping till.
items.description: Means "left," the opposite of right; shows up constantly in directions and in the compound 左右 (left and right).

example_sentences.japanese: 駅は左です。
example_sentences.english: The station is on the left.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]は左[ひだり]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 左に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go left.

example_sentences.furigana: 左[ひだり]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

items.mnemonic_text: A person (土-like legs) bounding forward: to run.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The signpost that's usually planted still in the <radical>earth</radical>, crossbar and flat soil baseline undisturbed for years, suddenly rips itself loose and bolts down the mountain trail, dragging a ragged tail of dirt behind it, going faster than a plain wooden post has any business going. Somehow, it is now running.
items.reading_mnemonic: Hikers at the top of the trail gasp <reading>そう</reading> — a drawn-out sound just like the English word <reading>sew</reading> — as the loose signpost sprints past the vending machine, and one startled hiker keeps repeating it long after the post is gone.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝公園を走ります。
example_sentences.english: I run in the park every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]公[こう]園[えん]を走[はし]ります。

items.mnemonic_text: A hand over a mouth, the right hand that feeds you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the flat horizon line of the <radical>ground</radical>, and a hand reaching down under it into an open <radical>mouth</radical> to pull something free — the fingers and the little box of the mouth locked together in one shape. That hand is always your dominant one, the one you shove in to grab a stuck snack. It's the hand on the right.
items.reading_mnemonic: You reach for the last onigiri on Koichi's shelf with your right hand and your fingers close on nothing but air, so you let out a soft "<reading>う</reading>う" of disappointment. That little "うう" is the sound you make when your right hand comes up empty.
items.description: 右, 左 and 石 all park something under a two-stroke top. 右 and 左 differ in what sits below: 右 has a small box, 左 a short cross-like piece. 石 shares 右's box but writes the top as a cliff, the horizontal running along the top with only its left end turning down.

example_sentences.japanese: トイレは右です。

example_sentences.furigana: トイレは右[みぎ]です。

items.mnemonic_text: Wings spread mid-motion: to fly.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character at once: two wings snapped open mid-beat, feathers combing the air on both sides, and a tail feather trailing straight back like it's still catching up. Nothing about the shape sits still — every stroke leans into the same direction, caught at the exact instant the ground lets go. That's fly.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a paper crane named <reading>Hee</reading> catches an updraft and lifts clean off the ground. She lets out one thin <reading>ひ</reading> of surprise and doesn't come back down before the trail bends out of sight.

example_sentences.japanese: 鳥が空を飛びます。
example_sentences.english: Birds fly in the sky.
example_sentences.furigana: 鳥[とり]が空[そら]を飛[と]びます。

example_sentences.furigana: 空[くう]港[こう]で飛[ひ]行[こう]機[き]を見[み]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) tangled in a tree (木): sunrise in the east.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <radical>sun</radical> rising and getting tangled in the branches of a <radical>tree</radical> on the horizon. You see the sun caught right behind that tree first thing in the morning — and the sun always comes up in the east. Sun plus tree, hung together at dawn: that's east.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker faces the sunrise and lets out a long, tired yawn — a huge "<reading>とう</reading>" that echoes down the slope. Every morning she climbs to greet the east with that same sleepy とう.

example_sentences.japanese: 東の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I open the east window.
example_sentences.furigana: 東[ひがし]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の東で友達に会いました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの町は東です。
example_sentences.english: That town is to the east.
example_sentences.furigana: あの町[まち]は東[ひがし]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A bird settling into its nest as the sun sets in the west.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a squat bird cage with a little bird perched inside, its legs dangling below the frame. At sunset the birds all fly home to roost, settling in the cage as the sun sinks in the same direction. That cage where everything comes to rest for the night points you toward the west.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, insists she always knows exactly where the sun sets, so she marches to the western edge of the sports field at dusk and points, calling out 「<reading>せい</reading>, that way!」 while the whole class watches the sky turn orange behind her.
items.description: 西 and 四 are both boxes with strokes inside. 四 is a plain rectangle with two short legs bending inward. 西 sits an extra horizontal bar across the very top, above the box, which 四 never has.

items.mnemonic_text: Bad luck (歹) beside a person collapsed: to die.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon is still airborne, gripping the bent <radical>spoon</radical> from that badly leveraged scoop of ice cream, and comes down hard on the already-cracked corner of <radical>death / bad luck</radical>. The bone gives way completely under the impact, nothing left to set or straighten. That's the whole story: die.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind the register at Koichi's konbini, the cashier named <reading>She</reading> hears the crash and doesn't even look up, just breathes one flat <reading>し</reading> and rings up the shattered tub anyway. Nothing about tonight is going to surprise her.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、猫が死にました。

example_sentences.furigana: この木[き]は冬[ふゆ]に死[し]にました。

items.mnemonic_text: A warm shelter facing the sunny south.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Somebody has upended a <radical>wide box</radical> on the hot sand, and across its flat top two matchsticks are laid in a <radical>cross</radical>, like the world's worst weather vane. A flamingo nudges the box round and round all afternoon, and the arm of the cross that ends up warmest is the one pointing south.
items.reading_mnemonic: A backpacker named Nan has been hiking down the mountain trail for days, always heading south toward warmer weather. Every time someone asks which way she's going, she just points and sighs, "<reading>なん</reading>... south, always south." The word なん sticks because Nan won't stop saying it.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の南は海です。
example_sentences.english: South of the station is the sea.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の南[みなみ]は海[うみ]です。

example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は南[みなみ]から来[き]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: A wandering road (辶) with a flag (斿) of fun: to play.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The bundled-up <radical>child</radical> flings both arms wide the moment its feet hit the ground and bolts straight past the crossroads signpost without reading a single <radical>direction</radical> off it, footsteps <radical>advance</radical>ing in zigzags down the winding road, chasing a moth, chasing nothing, laughing the whole way. Running in circles for no reason but joy: that is play.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at Koichi's konbini, a kid the clerk just calls <reading>You</reading> comes skidding in, sweaty from playing, and yells <reading>ゆう</reading> at every customer like it is a battle cry, delighted with himself, before running back out to play some more.

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は庭で犬と遊びます。
example_sentences.english: My little brother plays with the dog in the yard.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は庭[にわ]で犬[いぬ]と遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 金曜日の夜、友達と遊んだ。

items.mnemonic_text: Two people back to back turning away from the cold north.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon has finally landed. It came down in a snowdrift at the top of the map, still gripping the bent <radical>spoon</radical> it levered out of the ice cream tub, and it's now sitting back-to-back with a second raccoon on a frozen bench, both hunched away from each other against the gale — which is exactly the shape of this character. The <radical>spoon</radical> is frozen solid to its paws. That wind is coming straight down from the north.
items.reading_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, the wind off the northern peak is so brutal that a hiker named Hoku pulls his hood tight and mutters "<reading>ほく</reading>, ほく" through chattering teeth as he trudges. Hear him — ほく — every time you point north.

example_sentences.japanese: 北は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It is cold in the north.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 北から来ました。
example_sentences.english: I came from the north.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]から来[き]ました。

example_sentences.english: I will open the north window.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

items.mnemonic_text: Sheep (羊) settling onto the eye's (目) view: to arrive, to wear.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> arrives dragging a scratchy coat that snagged on its horns on the way over, plants its four stiff crossed legs on the doormat, and refuses to go one step further. The <radical>eye</radical> in the peephole, pupil pinched wide, watches the coat finally settle onto its back — the sheep has arrived, and now it is wearing the thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: At that same door, a courier named <reading>Chaku</reading> stamps the delivery slip and shouts <reading>ちゃく</reading> — arrived — before shoving the parcel at the sheep's hooves and speeding off, coat and all, without waiting for a signature.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は新しいシャツを着ます。
example_sentences.english: I'm wearing a new shirt today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は新[あたら]しいシャツを着[き]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 冬はいつもコートを着ます。
example_sentences.english: I always wear a coat in winter.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]はいつもコートを着[き]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は白い服を着ています。
example_sentences.english: Mom is wearing white clothes.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は白[しろ]い服[ふく]を着[き]ています。

items.mnemonic_text: A bird (隹) landing on a tree (木) with the flock: to gather.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Word gets out on some pigeon grapevine, and by dusk every <radical>old bird</radical> in town has shuffled onto the same <radical>tree</radical>, wings too stiff to fly, hopping branch to branch until the whole trunk is buried under molting, dust-covered old birds refusing to leave — the tree has gathered every last one of them.
items.reading_mnemonic: Up in the branches, an arborist swats at the crowd of old birds and yells <reading>Shoo</reading>, <reading>しゅう</reading>, but not one bird moves off the tree — there are too many, and shooing just isn't going to cut it today.

items.mnemonic_text: A lamp's flame steady atop its stand: the main, central one.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Three cheap flat <radical>king / jewel</radical> crowns wobble, skewered by one iron spike, and just as the pile threatens to slide off, a single <radical>drop</radical> of wax falls from the chandelier and seals the topmost crown in place. That fused, unmistakable stack is the one everyone bows to — the main one, the lord of the room.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back on the throne, the king's valet holds up the lord's one remaining polished <reading>shoe</reading> and announces <reading>しゅ</reading> to the court — the shoe proves who's still the main one in charge, wax-sealed crown and all.
items.description: 主 differs from 王 by exactly one mark: 主 adds a small drop stroke sitting above the top horizontal line, before the three stacked bars begin, while 王 has no dot at all — just the three flat crowns and the single spike through the middle, nothing above the topmost bar.

items.mnemonic_text: Power (力) worked in the rice field (田): a working man.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>rice field</radical> stretching out under the sun, and the one person out there doing the heavy lifting. He bends his arm, flexes his <radical>power</radical>, and drags the plow across the paddies all day. Someone with that much power working the rice field — that's the man.
items.reading_mnemonic: The man out in the field takes a break and starts pounding out a rhythm on his empty water bucket: <reading>だん</reading>, だん, だん. Every man on the trail can hear that drumbeat and grins.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) not yet (未) grown: the younger sister.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, the same crossed-limbed <radical>woman</radical> from the dance turns up tangled sideways in a <radical>tree</radical>, arms still flung wide, giggling and refusing to climb down until someone catches her — that reckless, easily rescued climber is your younger sister.
items.reading_mnemonic: Below her, someone shouts that she'll fall, and all she yells back, upside down and gleeful, is a stretched-out <reading>まい</reading> — <reading>my</reading> turn, not yet! — before slipping another branch lower.
items.description: Don't confuse this with 姉, the kanji for older sister. Here the right side is a tree with an extra short stroke near the top, giving two branches instead of one. The right side of 姉 instead stacks a lid over a hanging fold of cloth, a cap over drapery. Two branches is younger; cap-over-cloth is older.

items.mnemonic_text: Standing (立) by a tree (木) watching (見): a parent's love.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the edge of Sei's school field, someone has climbed a <radical>tree</radical> and wedged themselves upright to <radical>stand</radical> on the highest branch, craning forward to <radical>see</radical> every second of the match without missing a single kick — that worried, straining figure who won't leave until it's over is a parent.
items.reading_mnemonic: When the final whistle blows, they scramble down too fast and bark their <reading>しん</reading> — their <reading>shin</reading> — hard against a branch, then limp off still cheering about the goal.

items.mnemonic_text: A dangling shape on the side of the head: an ear.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and you'll spot a dangling shape hanging off the side of a head. That soft, drooping flap catching every sound is an <radical>ear</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A jittery DJ named Jiji cups a hand to his ear and shouts "<reading>じ</reading>, じ, do you hear that beat?" — the sound goes straight into his ear as じ.
items.description: Means "ear"; the body part, and shows up in words about hearing and listening.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) beside her child (子): a fondness, to like.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That bundled-up <radical>child</radical>, arms thrown wide, comes barreling down the konbini aisle and collides with the <radical>woman</radical> stocking the shelf, one leg still crossed mid-step from catching her balance. She doesn't scold him — she wraps her flung-wide arms around him and holds on, delighted. That's what liking someone looks like.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, watches from the till and tries to <reading>coax</reading> the toddler back with a sticker, murmuring <reading>こう</reading>, <reading>こう</reading> — but the kid's already found someone better to hug, so Koichi just restocks the onigiri instead.

items.mnemonic_text: A twisted shape over the heart (心): a bad feeling.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That same fishhook-shaped <radical>heart</radical>, still flinging its three drops of blood from the barb, gets swallowed whole by a stray cat behind the shrine. It doesn't turn the cat mean — it just makes everything the cat does afterward go wrong: knocked-over bins, hissing at nothing, one long streak of trouble. That's what a bad heart does.
items.reading_mnemonic: The cat, still hissing, gets its tail pinned under a fallen bin and yowls in pure <reading>awkward</reading> pain — <reading>あく</reading> — echoing off the shrine steps before it slinks away, guiltier than ever.

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth over stopping legs: a foot that carries you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>mouth</radical> perched on top of a pair of <radical>stopping</radical> legs — the legs have skidded to a halt, and the mouth is barking orders down at them. Those legs end in one thing: a <radical>foot</radical>. That mouth-over-stopping-legs shape is your foot, your leg, the thing you plant when you've had just enough.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker named Sok is nursing a blister on her foot. Every painful step she counts out loud, 「<reading>そく</reading>、そく、そく」, until she finally reaches the vending machine at the top and decides that's enough walking for one day.
items.description: Means foot, leg, or to suffice/be enough; shows up in words for body parts and in verbs about having sufficient amounts.

items.reading_mnemonic: Farmer <reading>Sai</reading> walks the paddy edge every morning, running a finger along the line to find it. Each time he loses sight of it in the grass he mutters <reading>さい</reading>, annoyed at how thin the thing is.

Its shadow swallows the whole window in one go, and the mossy steps drop into dark.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane fumbles for the huge bell in the sudden dark and rings it anyway, and from behind the cat a startled visitor named <reading>Anne</reading> gasps <reading>あん</reading>, あん, can't see a thing, groping past fur to find the steps.

items.mnemonic_text: A shelter (广) opening onto open ground: wide, spacious.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That cliffside <radical>shelter</radical> turns out to be absurdly wide — its diagonal roof floats over so much open air that a whole field fits underneath with room to spare. A silkworm tries to seal itself into a <radical>cocoon</radical> in one corner, spinning the closing loop again and again, but the space is too wide for it to ever meet the other edge. Wide.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi surveys his newly renovated konbini — the fluorescent aisles now stretch so wide he needs a golf cart to reach the onigiri shelf. He beams at the beeping till and announces, <reading>こう</reading>, this is what real square footage feels like, pure <reading>Koh</reading>-style efficiency at last.

Traffic idles as he turns something over, wrapping his cane-slow mind around a problem before taking another step. That's thinking.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, spots the old man frozen mid-crosswalk and can't restock the onigiri shelf until he moves. A crow on the awning tips its head and <reading>caws</reading> — <reading>こう</reading> — the exact sound of someone thinking too hard to hurry.

Investigate.

It keeps aiming for one bright bead of milk on a lilypad, glinting <radical>white</radical> in the sun. Attempt after attempt, feathers scattering, glint still out of reach — that relentless repeating is learn and practice.
items.reading_mnemonic: A birdwatcher named Shoe sits on the bank with a clipboard, tally marks climbing with every failed launch. She murmurs <reading>しゅう</reading>, <reading>Shoe</reading> under her breath at each attempt, certain the duckling will get airborne if it just keeps practicing.

items.mnemonic_text: A tree (木) crossed with mingling students: a school.

Your <radical>father</radical> has dragged the barbecue out under it, tongs held high in both hands, announcing lunch to four hundred children at once, and he's snapped the pot <radical>lid</radical> down over the grill by its little knob so the smoke doesn't set off the alarm in the hallway. Bells, classrooms, homework and dad grilling under the tree — this is school.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, has set up a pop-up shop right inside the school gate, restocking onigiri between classes and muttering <reading>こう</reading>, こう as he lines up the shelves. The kids buy their lunch from him before the bell.

items.mnemonic_text: A dying (亡) heart (心) losing its memory: to forget.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the wounded, thumping <radical>heart</radical> — hook dragging low, three drops flung off the barb — snags on a locker door and stops, mid-beat, whatever it was carrying draining out through the hook like the blood already has. By the time it works itself loose and wobbles on, it cannot recall what it snagged on. That blank, drained heart is forgetting.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down the empty hallway, a ghost named <reading>Bo</reading> drifts past the snagged heart and moans <reading>ぼう</reading>, low and hollow — the exact sound of something that used to matter fading out of a heart's grip entirely.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は今日、宿題を忘れました。
example_sentences.english: I forgot my homework today.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は今日[きょう]、宿[しゅく]題[だい]を忘[わす]れました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はいつも名前を忘れます。
example_sentences.english: She always forgets people's names.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はいつも名[な]前[まえ]を忘[わす]れます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは約束を忘れませんでした。
example_sentences.english: We didn't forget the appointment.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは約[やく]束[そく]を忘[わす]れませんでした。

items.mnemonic_text: A wagon (軍) moving down a road (辶): to carry, one's fortune.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, someone straps a tarp <radical>cover</radical> over the little <radical>vehicle</radical> — axle, two wheels — so nothing spills, then plants footstep after footstep to <radical>advance</radical> it up the steep climb toward the vending machine at the top. Whatever survives the grind, tarp still snug, wheels still spinning, has been carried — and just arriving on a slope like that counts as pure luck.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up, the hiker hauling the cart — everyone just calls her <reading>Oona</reading> — grunts <reading>うん</reading> with every step, the same sound as her own name, until the vending machine at the top rewards her stubbornness with a drink that isn't even the one she wanted.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝公園で運動する。
example_sentences.english: I exercise in the park every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]公[こう]園[えん]で運[うん]動[どう]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と一緒に荷物を運んだ。

items.mnemonic_text: Speech (言) with a mouth counting to five (五): words and language.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the left, <radical>words/speech</radical> is already pouring out — a <radical>mouth</radical> releasing stacked lines of speech. On the right, another open mouth joins in, adding its own noise. When mouths keep stacking speech on top of speech like this, what you get is a whole language, packed with word after word.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind the beeping till at Koichi's konbini, a chatty regular named Go won't stop talking — every single language pours out of him at once, and the only word you catch is his own name, <reading>ご</reading>, ご, ご.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と日本語で話します。
example_sentences.english: I speak with my friend in Japanese.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と日本[にほん]語[ご]で話[はな]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日日本語を勉強します。

example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]日本[にほん]語[ご]を勉[べん]強[きょう]します。

items.mnemonic_text: Two axes (斤斤) weighing shells (貝) of value: quality, substance.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The woodsman's <radical>axe</radical> is still buried hilt-deep in the chopping block — that argument's over. A peddler crouches beside it and pries the <radical>money</radical> shell open with both thumbs until coins spill into his palm, turning each one to the light, questioning it, weighing it, before he decides it has the quality worth the trade.
items.reading_mnemonic: The peddler pockets one more coin, but stump sawdust dusts his palm and it starts to itch. Sheesh, itchy, he hisses, shaking his hand out and blowing grit off the last coin, muttering <reading>しつ</reading>, <reading>しつ</reading> — the sound comes out exactly like his <reading>itchy</reading> complaint.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は質問があります。
example_sentences.english: I have a question.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は質[しつ]問[もん]があります。

items.mnemonic_text: Bamboo (竹) matching (合) the right response: an answer.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two stalks of <radical>bamboo</radical> in Sei's schoolyard lean together, leaves flicking like a drumroll. Right between their roots the level <radical>ground</radical> splits along one flat crack, and a wide square <radical>mouth</radical> yawns up out of the gap — not to ask anything, just to blurt out the answer before you've finished asking.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei stubs her toe on the bamboo root right where the ground cracked open, and yelps instead of answering the teacher's question. Everyone laughs, but the barked <reading>とう</reading> still counts — a stubbed <reading>toe</reading> makes exactly that sound, and gets treated as her answer anyway.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は先生の質問に答えました。
example_sentences.english: I answered the teacher's question.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は先[せん]生[せい]の質[しつ]問[もん]に答[こた]えました。

example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は質[しつ]問[もん]にすぐ答[こた]えました。

items.mnemonic_text: A flag (方 side) rallying an arrow's (矢) clan together: family.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That same stray <radical>arrow</radical>, still quivering in the vendor's pumpkin, turns out to be signed — feathers dyed the same color every year. Uncles, cousins, and a very unbothered grandmother converge on the fence from every <radical>direction</radical> the crossroads signpost names, each recognizing the fletching as theirs, until a whole clan is arguing over one ruined pumpkin about whose family shot it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma stomps up in mismatched <reading>socks</reading>, glaring at the ruined pumpkin, and mutters <reading>ぞく</reading> under her breath before anyone else speaks — the whole family already knows exactly which cousin's arrow this is, just from the socks.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の家族は五人です。
example_sentences.english: There are five people in my family.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の家[か]族[ぞく]は五[ご]人[にん]です。

example_sentences.english: My family eats dinner together every night.

items.mnemonic_text: Rice (米) measured with a dipper (斗): materials, a fee.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the baker plunges the trusted <radical>dipper</radical> into a sack of <radical>rice</radical>, its grains scattering like a tiny explosion as it comes up loaded and level. He tips it into a paper bag, marks a tally on the register, and charges by the scoop — the material measured out becomes exactly the fee you pay.
items.reading_mnemonic: A customer named <reading>Leo</reading> counts each dipper-load of rice as it clinks into his bag, muttering <reading>りょう</reading>, <reading>りょう</reading> under his breath to keep track of how many scoops he owes, until his tally and the register's total match up, scoop for scoop.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日料理します。
example_sentences.english: I cook every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]料[りょう]理[り]します。

items.mnemonic_text: A heart (心) pierced by a single resolved stroke: certainly necessary.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>heart</radical> is still hooked low and flinging its three drops of blood when a cleaver comes down and pins it flat to the altar with one diagonal slash through the middle. Nobody moves it again — a heart nailed down like that isn't optional anymore, it's simply necessary.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shrine boy who nailed it down mutters a chant over the pinned heart, tapping the blade's handle twice for luck, and it comes out as a flat little <reading>ひつ</reading> — like he's clearing his throat, <reading>hit-soo</reading>, before he can walk away.
items.description: 必 is 心 (heart) with one extra diagonal stroke slashing down across the hook from upper left to lower right. Without that slash, the three loose drops sit under a bare fishhook — that plain shape is 心 on its own. With it, the stroke pins straight through the hook, and that pinned, slashed heart is 必.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝必ずコーヒーを飲みます。

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) under a covering (覀): the essential point, needed.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The talent show can't start without her: the <radical>woman</radical> frozen mid-dance, one leg swung wide and arms flung across her body, is the only act the whole gym is waiting on. Every other performer gets cut from the lineup before her, because without that one dancer nothing here is important enough to keep.
items.reading_mnemonic: Backstage, the stage manager keeps checking his clipboard and groaning <reading>よう</reading>, the same sound he'd make chasing a lost <reading>yo-yo</reading> under the bleachers, because the dancer still hasn't shown up and the whole show needs her.

items.mnemonic_text: Two people standing side by side: to compare.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Outside Koichi's konbini, two identical clerks stand shoulder to shoulder against the doorframe, backs flat, chins level, each daring the other to be an inch taller. Neither moves, neither blinks — they just stand there side by side under the fluorescent light, forever being compared.
items.reading_mnemonic: One clerk finally cracks and jabs a thumb at himself, shouting <reading>ひ</reading> — insisting <reading>He</reading>'s obviously the taller one — while the other clerk just narrows his eyes and keeps standing there under the konbini lights, refusing to concede an inch.
items.description: 比 almost never stands alone as a word. In everyday use it shows up bound into other kanji or attached as 比べる, and mostly in contexts about ratios and percentages rather than as a freestanding term by itself.

items.mnemonic_text: A foot planted firmly: stop.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You're mid-stride down the mountain trail when you plant one foot flat and hard against the ground and freeze in place. That single planted foot is the whole picture: it's rooted, going nowhere. A planted foot means <radical>stop</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Right where you stopped, you hear a sharp "<reading>し</reading>!" — someone shushing you. It's the vending machine at the top of the trail, hissing "し, し" as it refuses to dispense until you stop and wait. That shushing し is the sound to hold onto.
items.description: Means "stop" and is the base of common verbs like 止まる and 止める, showing up anywhere something halts or is brought to a halt.

items.mnemonic_text: Feet advancing (辶) among matched (巽) options: to choose.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail is the same winding <radical>road</radical> you've been climbing, footsteps advancing step by step toward the summit — except today it forks three ways around the vending machine. You plant one foot on a single fork and commit, ignoring the other two. Deciding which path to advance down is what it means to choose.
items.reading_mnemonic: At that same fork, a hiker named <reading>Sen</reading> freezes completely, muttering <reading>せん</reading> over and over while staring at the vending machine, unable to advance a single step until he finally commits to a path.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は静かな部屋を選びました。
example_sentences.english: I chose a quiet room.

items.mnemonic_text: A person standing on the ground line: to stand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person planted firmly on the ground, feet apart, refusing to budge — they <radical>stand</radical> there, solid and upright. That single image, a person rooted on the earth, is the whole character: to stand.
items.reading_mnemonic: A soldier named Ritsu snaps to attention on the mountain trail, standing so straight you could measure a wall against him. Every time someone shouts "<reading>りつ</reading>!" he stands up even taller.
items.description: Means "stand"; a common N5 kanji appearing in words about standing up, standing something upright, and establishing or setting things in place.

items.mnemonic_text: Two people (人) sitting on the earth (土) under a roof.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two of those striding <radical>person</radical> figures come in from the cold, legs still mid-stride, and drop straight down onto the same patch of <radical>earth</radical> at the foot of the signpost. They plant themselves on that soil, shoulder to shoulder, and flatly refuse to get up again. When two walkers settle onto the earth like that, all they want to do is sit.
items.reading_mnemonic: The person who settles onto that patch of earth is Zara, and the moment she sits she lets out a long, satisfied "<reading>ざ</reading>あ" of relief. Every time you see someone plop down here, you hear Zara's ざ.
items.description: Means "sit"; shows up in words about sitting down, seats, and taking a seat.

example_sentences.furigana: 誰[だれ]がここに座[すわ]りましたか。

items.mnemonic_text: A person (人) leaning on a tree (木): resting.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You're on the mountain trail and you spot a <radical>person</radical> (left) who has slumped sideways against a <radical>tree</radical>, leaning into the trunk with its roots and branches like it's the comfiest chair in the world. A <radical>person</radical> plus a tree they're propped against — that's someone taking a well-earned rest.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker leaning on that tree lets out a huge, happy sigh — "<reading>きゅう</reading>!" — the sound of every muscle finally letting go. Every time you picture that person melting into rest, you hear that きゅう escape.
items.description: Means "rest" and shows up in everyday words for taking breaks and days off, like 休み.

example_sentences.english: I will take a day off from work tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、仕[し]事[ごと]を休[やす]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: ここでちょっと休みましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's rest here for a bit.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the bottom of this character and you'll find a <radical>mouth</radical>, wide open. Above it, stacked up in neat horizontal lines, is everything that mouth is pushing out — layer after layer of <radical>speech</radical>. A mouth releasing stacked lines like that is exactly what it means to say a word.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a general in full armor climbs the mossy steps and won't stop giving orders — every word out of his mouth is a barked command. The cats scatter as the general says "<reading>げん</reading>!" like it's the only word he knows.

example_sentences.english: What did the teacher say?
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は何[なに]と言[い]いましたか。

items.mnemonic_text: A dog (犬) squeezing back under a door (戸): to return.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That raccoon that rammed shoulder-first through the <radical>door</radical>, scraping its tail on the sill as it barreled into the kitchen, doesn't stop there. It circles the block, and twenty minutes later barges back through that same battered door, right where it started, tail scraping the sill all over again. That's return.
items.reading_mnemonic: Next door, a neighbor named Ray sighs <reading>れい</reading> every time he hears the door bang, flat and resigned, like counting the raccoon's laps with a low '<reading>ray</reading>'. Sure enough, a beat later, it barrels back through, right on cue.
items.description: This kanji's on'yomi is genuinely rare in modern Japanese. Outside a handful of fixed compounds, it overwhelmingly appears with its kun'yomi reading instead, so lean on that reading first in real text you encounter.

items.mnemonic_text: Horns flaring above a frame of stiff crossed legs: a sheep.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the shape and you'll find nothing new in it: two short strokes flaring out at the top like horns, and a frame beneath locked into four stiff crossed legs. Not one stroke has been added to the <radical>sheep</radical> you already know. Standing on its own, unchanged and unbothered, it is simply a sheep.
items.reading_mnemonic: The flock's leader shoulders through the door of Koichi's konbini like a regular, and Koichi barely glances up before giving it the usual greeting: "<reading>よう</reading>!" The sheep bleats it straight back at him, <reading>よう</reading>, and heads for the onigiri shelf.

example_sentences.japanese: あの山に白い羊がたくさんいます。
example_sentences.english: There are a lot of white sheep on that mountain.
example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]に白[しろ]い羊[ひつじ]がたくさんいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昼ご飯に羊の肉を食べました。
example_sentences.english: I had lamb for lunch.
example_sentences.furigana: 昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]に羊[ひつじ]の肉[にく]を食[た]べました。

example_sentences.japanese: 羊が道の真ん中に立っています。
example_sentences.english: A sheep is standing in the middle of the road.
example_sentences.furigana: 羊[ひつじ]が道[みち]の真[ま]ん中[なか]に立[た]っています。

items.mnemonic_text: A fresh sprout over the moon: the blue-green of youth.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a tiny sprout pushing up over the <radical>moon</radical>. It's young, fresh, and glowing that impossible color between <radical>blue</radical> and green — the shade of new leaves at dusk. That youthful sprout-over-moon is blue-green.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, holds up a jar of blue-green ink and says the color is called 「<reading>せい</reading>」 — of course she knew it first. She's already dipping her perfect brush in before anyone else can answer.
items.description: Means blue or green (the fresh blue-green range); shows up in color words and in compounds about youth and freshness.

example_sentences.japanese: あの青いペンを借りました。
example_sentences.english: I borrowed that blue pen.
example_sentences.furigana: あの青[あお]いペンを借[か]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい青い車を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a new blue car.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい青[あお]い車[くるま]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 青と白の服を着ます。
example_sentences.english: I will wear blue and white clothes.
example_sentences.furigana: 青[あお]と白[しろ]の服[ふく]を着[き]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: A tall tower with windows: high and expensive.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>tall</radical> tower with windows standing over the town — but notice the open <radical>mouth</radical> at its base, an entrance yawning wide for anyone brave enough to climb. It's the fanciest, most expensive building around, and everyone cranes their neck to see how tall it is.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, is jealous of that tall tower, so he stacks his onigiri shelves higher and higher until they're the tallest — and priciest — display in town. As the tower of rice balls wobbles, he shouts <reading>こう</reading> to warn a customer before it topples.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、高い時計を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought an expensive watch yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、高[たか]い時計[とけい]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの山は高いです。
example_sentences.english: That mountain over there is tall.
example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]は高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: あのレストランの肉は高いです。
example_sentences.english: The meat at that restaurant is expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: あのレストランの肉[にく]は高[たか]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: A standing tree cut by an axe (斤): freshly new.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>spicy</radical> man hauls his pepper skewer into the showroom, eyes streaming, hat still riding its column of sweat, swearing the sauce is mild. Behind him a <radical>tree</radical> sits on the plinth, dug up roots and all, sap still wet where the branch was cut this morning, and the person on the platform is <radical>standing</radical> beside it with both arms thrown out so nobody touches anything. Just cut, just picked, just unwrapped — everything in here is new.
items.reading_mnemonic: The showroom greeter is Shin, and every time a new model rolls in he shouts his own name — <reading>しん</reading>! — as he yanks the cover off. Whatever Shin unveils is always brand new.
items.description: Means "new"; a very common kanji appearing in words for new things, newspapers, and freshness.

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい車を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a new car.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい車[くるま]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 父は毎朝新聞を読みます。
example_sentences.english: My father reads the newspaper every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]新[しん]聞[ぶん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: あの新しいレストランはおいしいです。
example_sentences.english: That new restaurant is delicious.
example_sentences.furigana: あの新[あたら]しいレストランはおいしいです。

items.mnemonic_text: Ten (十) mouths (口) of stories passed down: old.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Above the <radical>mouth</radical> balances a little <radical>cross</radical> of stacked crossbars, like the beams of a house that's been standing for centuries. Every mouth that has passed through here has told the same worn-out story, over and over. A mouth held up by ancient timber can only mean one thing: old.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi finds an ancient rice ball at the very back of his konbini shelf, so far past its date the wrapper has yellowed. He picks it up, sighs, and mutters just one syllable at how old it is: 「<reading>こ</reading>」.
items.description: Means "old," as in old and worn from age; appears in words about age and antiquity and in the common word for "used/secondhand."

example_sentences.japanese: 古い車を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought an old car.
example_sentences.furigana: 古[ふる]い車[くるま]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: この町には古い家がたくさんあります。
example_sentences.english: There are a lot of old houses in this town.
example_sentences.furigana: この町[まち]には古[ふる]い家[いえ]がたくさんあります。

example_sentences.japanese: その時計は少し古いです。
example_sentences.english: That watch is a little old.
example_sentences.furigana: その時計[とけい]は少[すこ]し古[ふる]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: Drops falling inside a window frame from the sky: rain.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look through the window frame and watch the drops falling inside it, one after another down the glass. Those little drops caught in the frame are all you need to picture. Drops falling inside a window frame: <radical>rain</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cow gets caught outside in the downpour and lets out a long, miserable "<reading>う</reading>ー" as the drops soak her. Every time it rains, that cow's soggy うー is the sound you hear.
items.description: Means "rain"; the base kanji for weather words and it sits on top of many other weather-related characters as a component.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日はたくさん雨が降りました。
example_sentences.english: It rained a lot yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]はたくさん雨[あめ]が降[ふ]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は雨が嫌いです。
example_sentences.english: I dislike rain.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は雨[あめ]が嫌[きら]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は雨ですか。
example_sentences.english: Will it rain tomorrow?
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は雨[あめ]ですか。

items.mnemonic_text: A horse (馬) waiting where trains stop: a station.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You're waiting on a platform when a galloping <radical>horse</radical>, flowing mane and all four legs pounding, thunders straight past you and onto the tracks. The conductor sighs — this happens every day here, horses treating the place like a pasture. Where else would a runaway horse end up but the station?
items.reading_mnemonic: A commuter named Eki misses the last train and shouts "<reading>えき</reading>! えき!" across the empty platform, hoping the station master will hear her and hold the doors.
items.description: Means "station" — the word for a train or subway station, seen constantly in place names and on transit signs.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅は家から近いです。
example_sentences.english: The station is close to my house.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]は家[いえ]から近[ちか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅員に切符を見せます。
example_sentences.english: I show my ticket to the station staff.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]員[いん]に切[きっ]符[ぷ]を見[み]せます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝この駅で電車に乗ります。
example_sentences.english: I board the train at this station every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]この駅[えき]で電[でん]車[しゃ]に乗[の]ります。

items.mnemonic_text: A neck (首) moving down a path: the road and the way.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The giraffe in the business suit is late, so it lowers its telescoping <radical>neck</radical> flat to the ground and lets the winding <radical>road</radical> unroll straight along the top of it, spots and all. Commuters simply walk up the giraffe and keep going, and by lunchtime nobody can tell where the animal ends and the way forward begins — this kanji is road, the way.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the road you meet a doe standing in the middle of the path, blocking the way. She won't budge, so you call out "<reading>どう</reading> do I get past you?" — and the doe just chews and stares, owning the whole road.
items.description: Means road or way; a very common kanji seen in words for streets, paths, and figurative "ways" of doing things.

example_sentences.japanese: この道は長いです。
example_sentences.english: This road is long.
example_sentences.furigana: この道[みち]は長[なが]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日道を歩きます。
example_sentences.english: I walk along the road every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]道[みち]を歩[ある]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 道の近くに公園があります。
example_sentences.english: There's a park near the road.
example_sentences.furigana: 道[みち]の近[ちか]くに公[こう]園[えん]があります。

items.mnemonic_text: A rice field (田) marked out into a town.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture this whole character as a bird's-eye view of a settlement: a neat grid of <radical>rice fields</radical> on the left pressed up against a straight main road running down the right. Fields plus a road is the smallest complete place people can live in — that's a town.
items.reading_mnemonic: The town mayor climbs onto a soapbox in the square and announces he's the big chief now: "I'm in charge — call me <reading>ちょう</reading>!" Every time you walk into this town, you hear that same booming ちょう echoing off the buildings.
items.description: Means "town" and shows up in place names and words for local districts and neighborhoods.

example_sentences.japanese: この町は賑やかです。
example_sentences.english: This town is lively.
example_sentences.furigana: この町[まち]は賑[にぎ]やかです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、町へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow I'm going to town.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、町[まち]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はこの町に住んでいます。
example_sentences.english: He lives in this town.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]はこの町[まち]に住[す]んでいます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> at the left, and beside her the whole shape of <radical>stopping</radical>: the eye that has seen something and the foot that will not take another step. She is planted in the doorway with her arms folded, and the young one is not going out tonight. A girl who gets stopped at the door is somebody's <radical>daughter</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Jou is how the neighbours refer to her, drawn out and a shade too formal — 「<reading>じょう</reading>」 — the sort of address you use for a girl of good family who is very definitely not allowed out. She hears じょう and rolls her eyes.

items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Rain</radical> across the whole top of the character, and underneath it a <radical>person</radical> kneeling on the bare <radical>ground</radical> while the clerk presses her <radical>stamp</radical> down onto the ledger. It lands in the column where this year's crop should have been counted, and what it prints there is one perfect round <radical>zero</radical>. The rain took the lot.
items.reading_mnemonic: Rei is that clerk. She is scrupulously polite about it — a small bow, a murmured 「<reading>れい</reading>」 — and then she inks the nothing into your row and moves down the line. れい, bow, zero. She has done it forty times today.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> stands at the far left, and stacked up beside him is a <radical>big</radical> load: a <radical>sheep</radical> he has to carry in, then <radical>split</radical> into portions for everyone else before he takes any himself. He does the hauling and he eats last, and when he speaks he uses the humble word for <radical>me</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Boku is the errand boy who answers every question about who did it with the same word: 「<reading>ぼく</reading>」. Broke the gate? ぼく. Carried the sheep up the hill? ぼく. He never says his own name, so ぼく is the only name you have for him.
